page6_img_1.png.title: Per-program distribution of type shapes (atomic vs linear vs cyclic)
page6_img_1.png.description: Stacked bars show, for each DaCapo program (antlr, avrora, chart, fop, h2, luindex, lusearch, pmd, sunflow, xalan), the fraction of instantiated types whose abstracted shape is atomic, linear, or cyclic (y‑axis 0.0–1.0). In every program the atomic category (the dominant mid-gray band) comprises the large majority of types; linear shapes form a thin band in most programs and cyclic shapes (the darker band) are noticeable only in a few cases (notably antlr and pmd). This visual pattern matches the paper’s measurements: atomic shapes average about 85% ± 12% of types, and cyclic shapes occur significantly more often than linear shapes (p = 0.03).

page7_img_1.png.title: Violin plots of in-degree distributions per type and per component
page7_img_1.png.description: Two side-by-side violin plots show the distribution of in-degree (number of distinct incoming abstract edges) across retained heap snapshots for each DaCapo program: (a) per type and (b) per conceptual component. Both plots concentrate strongly at low in-degree (medians near 1), indicating most types and components are referenced from only one place, but several benchmarks (notably antlr, xalan and fop) have long, heavy tails. The component plot (right) uses a logarithmic vertical scale and reveals extreme outliers — some components receive dozens to hundreds of incoming edges — which the paper attributes to large recursive structures and many unique objects stored in containers (e.g., dictionaries). Overall the figures support the paper’s claim that while local ownership is common, a non-trivial number of types/components exhibit high in-degree and thus significant sharing.

page8_img_1.png.title: Injectivity and sharing breakdown per field and per component edge
page8_img_1.png.description: Two stacked-bar charts compare, for ten DaCapo programs (antlr, avrora, chart, fop, h2, luindex, lusearch, pmd, sunflow, xalan), the fraction of pointers that are injective versus various classes of non-injective sharing. The left chart (a) shows the breakdown per program field and the right chart (b) shows the breakdown per abstract component edge, with the y-axis as a proportion from 0 to 1. In both charts the lightest band (Injective) dominates most programs — overall about 87%–96% of fields and about 90%–99% of edges are injective — while the remaining non-injective portion is mostly Immutable (dark gray), with smaller contributions from Singleton and Globally Shared, and a small Unclassified fraction (black). A few benchmarks (notably avrora and fop) exhibit noticeably larger non-injective/unclassified portions, but in general injective pointers comprise the vast majority of both fields and component edges.

page3_img_1.png.title: Concrete and abstract heap: expression tree components and sharing
page3_img_1.png.description: The top diagram (a) is a concrete heap snapshot: a local root exp points to an Add node whose l and r fields link into a small expression tree (Add, Mult, Sub, Const), and a static env root points to a Var[3] array whose indices [0],[1] reference two Var objects that are also referenced from the expression nodes. The bottom diagram (b) is the HeapDbg abstraction collapsing concrete objects into four conceptual components: $1 {Add, Mult, Sub} with a self-loop labeled tree(l,r), $2 {Var}, $3 {Const}, and $4 {Var[]}; labeled edges (l, r, []) connect these components. The Var component $2 has multiple incoming (cross) edges (highlighted) from both $1 and $4 indicating shared references, whereas the Const component $3 is reached by a single injective r edge (i.e., locally owned).

page9_img_table_1.png.title: Sharing classification of fields and component edges across benchmarks
page9_img_table_1.png.description: A tabular breakdown (per program and overall confidence intervals) of how pointer relations in the abstracted heaps are classified: top sections report the fraction of fields and component edges that are Tree, Cross, or Back edges; lower sections split Cross edges/fields by idioms (Contained, Global, Unique, Immutable, Unclassified). The table shows Tree is the dominant category for most programs (per-field Tree CI 49%–71%; per-edge Tree CI 53%–75%), Cross is the second-most common (per-edge CI 21%–37%), and Back edges are usually small (per-edge CI 1%–11%) though some programs (e.g., avrora) are outliers. For Cross sharing, Immutable targets are the largest subclass (cross-field CI 6%–15%; cross-edge CI 7%–16%), Contained sharing accounts for a few percent (fields 4%–8%, edges 2%–6%), Unique and Global are rare, and the remaining Unclassified sharing is modest (fields CI 8%–15%, edges CI 7%–18%).

page7_img_2.png.title: Pointer properties per program: internal, non-null, and local-owner percentages
page7_img_2.png.description: Two side-by-side bar charts compare three pointer properties for ten DaCapo programs (antlr, avrora, chart, fop, h2, luindex, lusearch, pmd, sunflow, xalan): (a) percentages per field and (b) percentages per conceptual-component edge. For each program the three bars show the fraction (0–1.0 on the y-axis) of pointers that are internal (dark, small bars), non-null (tall gray bars) and owners / locally-owning (outlined white bars). The plots show that non-null pointers dominate across all programs (most values roughly 0.7–0.95), owner pointers are substantial but variable between programs (consistent with the paper’s average ≈50% of fields being local owners, 95% CI ≈39%–63%), and internal pointers are relatively rare (near zero in most cases). Notable program differences appear (for example, avrora has relatively low owner rates per field, while sunflow shows high owner rates), illustrating the per-benchmark variation behind the reported averages.
